hops.title: Why a stubbed toe hurts twice
hops.text: If you have ever caught a bare toe on a doorframe, you may remember the timing. First comes a sharp sting. A moment later, a slow burning ache rolls in. One bump activates two kinds of pain fiber in the toe, and they report at different speeds. The sharp first pain rides thinly myelinated fibers at about 10 to 15 meters per second. The burn travels on thin unmyelinated axons, held together in Remak bundles, at roughly 0.5 to 2 meters per second. Over the length of a leg, that speed difference is enough to split one accident into two sensations you can tell apart.

image.caption: One stubbed toe, two pains: thinly myelinated fibers bring the sting, slower unmyelinated Remak-bundle fibers bring the burn.

hops.title: How Mycobacterium leprae switches on ErbB2 by itself
hops.text: During peripheral myelination, ErbB2 on a Schwann cell has no ligand of its own; it is activated when ErbB3 reads neuregulin-1 from the axon. Mycobacterium leprae, the main cause of leprosy, can bypass that handshake. In 2006 researchers reported that, in experimental models, the bacterium bound directly to ErbB2 without needing ErbB3 or neuregulin-1 and switched on signaling that damaged myelin. One line of evidence that this signaling drove the damage in those models: PKI-166, a small-molecule drug that blocks the kinase activity of ErbB2 and its relative ErbB1, reduced myelin breakdown both in cell culture and in mice.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A quiet lab bench with a microscope, two glass culture dishes, a small glass bottle of powder, and a blank notebook.
image.caption: In experimental models, Mycobacterium leprae activated Schwann-cell ErbB2 directly, and the dual ErbB2/ErbB1 kinase inhibitor PKI-166 reduced myelin damage.

hops.title: Uhthoff's exercise clue and the hot-bath test
hops.text: In 1890 the German ophthalmologist Wilhelm Uhthoff described something odd in four patients with multiple sclerosis: after physical exertion, their vision temporarily dimmed. Uhthoff tied it to exertion. Later work showed that a rise in body temperature brings on the same kind of short-lived worsening, and starting in the 1950s doctors turned that heat sensitivity into a hot-bath test for diagnosing the disease, a practice that gave way to MRI and spinal-fluid tests during the 1980s. Losing myelin leaves axons with such a slim conduction margin that even modest warming can temporarily block their signals until the body cools back down.

sources.citation: Panginikkod et al., Uhthoff Phenomenon, StatPearls (2022).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A steaming vintage clawfoot bathtub in a quiet tiled room beside a wooden stool holding a folded towel, a glass thermometer and round spectacles.
image.caption: Demyelinated axons conduct with so little margin that modest warming can briefly block them, the basis of the hot-bath test.
